title: What Canada and Australia teach the UK about constitutional safeguards
label: 28 October 2026 · Comparative evidence session
summary: Two constitutional scholars from Australia and Canada explained how their written, federal constitutions and institutions protect democracy, compared to the UK's partly-unwritten system. They emphasised that laws and courts help, but culture and political behaviour are crucial; warned about executive overreach, delegation and financial tensions in federations; and highlighted specific safeguards—compulsory voting (Australia), entrenched rights and judicial review, indigenous legal traditions (Canada), independent offices and anti-corruption bodies—and the limits of any legal fix without civic responsibility. A recent Canadian emergency-declaration dispute and Australia’s secret ministries episode were cited as tests of those safeguards.

glossary.definition: A written constitution that can only be changed using special procedures, like a referendum, not by ordinary laws.
A legal requirement that eligible people must attend polling stations to vote in elections.
A direct vote by the electorate on a specific constitutional or political question.
Courts' ability to strike down laws that conflict with the constitution.
The division of government into branches (executive, legislature, judiciary) to prevent concentration of power.
Powers historically held by the Crown or executive that are exercised without new parliamentary legislation.
In Australia, a constitutional protection inferred by courts that prevents laws blocking political speech.
Provisions that let Ministers change or override primary legislation using secondary rules, reducing parliamentary oversight.
Laws that allow governments to take special powers in crises; their use can be legally contested.

chapters.title: How Canada and Australia compare with the UK
chapters.takeaway: Canada and Australia share British political traditions but differ mainly by having written, federal constitutions and stronger judicial review.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please explain the main similarities and differences between the UK, Canada and Australia on constitutional safeguards.

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Canada and Australia inherited many UK features: the prerogative, responsible government, parliamentary procedures. But both are federations with written constitutions that courts can enforce. That makes judicial invalidation of laws possible in ways the UK doesn’t have.

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: I agree. Canada is a federation and a plurinational settler state. It has a written constitution, plus a resurgence of indigenous legal traditions now recognised by courts, which adds extra constitutional safeguards and perspectives.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You mentioned indigenous constitutionalism — is it written or oral?

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: Many traditions were oral, but as courts and modern institutions apply them, communities increasingly record their customs in writing to participate in legal processes.

chapters.title: What actually protects democracy?
chapters.takeaway: Laws and institutions matter, but the behaviour and culture of politicians and the public are decisive safeguards.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: Which safeguards are most important, and can the UK learn from Canada or Australia?

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: Written rights, judicial review and independent bodies help, but none are self-executing. The system relies on political actors internalising norms. When they don't, even written constitutions can fail, as recent events in other countries show.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: So it's the 'good-chap' theory—if leaders behave badly, institutions won't save you?

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: Yes. The ultimate backstop is the electorate. Courts and institutions help, but they can't alone prevent democratic backsliding if political actors disregard norms.

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: I agree, but structural safeguards help. An entrenched constitution that secures separation of powers, guarantees elections and protects political speech makes it harder for an executive to entrench itself.

chapters.title: Compulsory voting and civic education
chapters.takeaway: Australia’s compulsory voting drives broad turnout and tends to moderate politics, though civic education remains important.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: How does compulsory voting affect politics and civic education in Australia?

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Compulsory voting brings the political centre to the polls and reduces extreme distortions. It makes parties aim policies broadly and keeps turnout high, which discourages polarisation.

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: But our civics education could be better. Compulsory voting forces people to pay attention, but schools should still teach constitutional basics and how government works.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Would Australia resist dropping compulsory voting?

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Yes—it's popular. People see it as a civic duty. It would be politically difficult to remove.

chapters.title: Entrenchment, rights and parliamentary oversight
chapters.takeaway: Entrenched constitutional provisions and judicial review protect core democratic rules, but who oversees government matters: Parliament or the Executive—varies and matters a lot.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: Is there any system that can prevent an elected leader from disregarding constitutional norms?

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: No single design will prevent abuse. Canada has rights, federalism, independent officers and judicial review, but these only work if political actors respect norms. Courts have limits and are unelected.

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Australia lacks a full bill of rights because people worry about shifting many policy choices to judges. So we favour entrenching the rules that stop abuse—who votes, election timing, separation of powers—while leaving social policy to parliaments.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: How did Australia decide what to entrench?

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Entrenchment flowed from creating a federation: you must lock in some rules. It took years of debate historically. For new entrenchments now, the process matters—don’t let a simple majority entrench something that only a referendum can remove.

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Look at state constitutions: some parts can be changed by ordinary laws, others need referendums. If you entrench rules, you should require the same seriousness to change them as to create them.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: What about parliamentary scrutiny—does Canada do anything the UK could copy?

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: Canada has strong pre-enactment rights reviews in the Executive, and 'charter statements' for legislation, but Parliament largely depends on the Executive for constitutional advice. The UK’s Constitution Committee model with independent advisers is something Canada could learn from to strengthen parliamentary oversight.

chapters.title: Threats, examples and practical fixes
chapters.takeaway: Executive overreach, financial tensions in federations, excessive delegation and weak scrutiny are the real dangers; independent institutions and cultural respect for rule of law are key defenses.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Burry Port
turns.text: As we consider more devolution, what practical problems should we watch for?

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Money is the toughest part of federalism. How funds are shared creates the most conflict. Also watch excessive delegation to the Executive, Henry VIII clauses, and prorogation: Parliament must keep control over spending and delegated powers.

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Independent offices—anti-corruption commissions, auditors-general, ombudsmen—act as a 'fourth branch' to check power and are valuable safeguards.

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: Democracies face external pressures—pandemic, AI, cost of living—that stress institutions. A recent Canadian test: the 2022 trucker convoy led to an emergencies declaration, then a commission and conflicting court rulings. The case is now before the Supreme Court.

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: In Australia, public outrage stopped an obvious abuse: the former PM's secret ministerial appointments during COVID were exposed and criticised, showing culture and accountability matter.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: So are courts the main remedy?

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: Courts are essential, but limited. They interpret rules after the fact. The strongest defence is a combination of institutions, civic action and political responsibility.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final practical advice for the UK?

turns.speaker: Professor Anne Twomey
turns.text: Protect parliamentary powers over spending and delegated legislation, guard judicial independence, consider entrenching key democratic rules carefully, and strengthen independent oversight bodies.

turns.speaker: Professor Vanessa MacDonnell
turns.text: Add clearer parliamentary access to independent constitutional advice, recognise diversity of legal traditions where relevant, and remember that structural reforms must be paired with efforts to maintain a culture of constitutional respect.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. Your comparative insights—legal rules, institutions and the limits of law alone—are much appreciated.
